children.text: Mount Tapyas is the hill rising right behind Coron town. Climb about 720 concrete steps and, beyond a giant white cross and the CORON letters, you take in Coron Bay, the limestone cliffs of Coron Island and Uson Island all at once. With no entrance fee and an easy walk from town, it is Coron's signature viewpoint, where travelers head for the sunset after a day of island hopping.

Mount Tapyas is a small peak that rises straight up where the center of Coron town ends, at the southeastern tip of Busuanga Island. Its height is given differently from source to source, somewhere around

, but with the town and the sea right below your feet it feels far higher than that. The concrete stairway that starts beside a basketball court at the foot of the hill has about 720 steps (721 or 724, depending on the source), with handrails and rest stops with benches along the way, so anyone in a pair of sneakers can make it up.

At the top stand a giant white steel-frame cross and a broad concrete viewing deck, and just below the summit, on the slope, white CORON letters stand in the style of the Hollywood sign. After dark the cross and the letters light up, so you can pick out the hill clearly from town and even from boats on the water. From the deck, the rooftops of Coron town, the port, Coron Bay dotted with bangka boats and, beyond them, the limestone cliffs of Coron Island, home to Kayangan Lake and Twin Lagoon, spread out in a full panorama.

The name "tapyas" is said to mean "to chip off" or "to cut away" in the local language. One explanation is that it comes from the flattened shape of the summit; another story says that during World War II, US planes bombed the hill where Japanese soldiers were hiding and knocked off its top. Neither has been confirmed by official records, so take them as fun local legends. Since Coron is famous for diving on the Japanese warship wrecks lying on the floor of Coron Bay, stories like this attach themselves naturally.
There is no entrance or parking fee, and from most hotels in town the foot of the stairs is a
10–15-minute

walk. That is why island hopping by day and climbing up here at dusk for the sunset has become the standard way to end a day in Coron. Travel agencies' Coron town tours almost always include it too, along with Lualhati Park and Maquinit Hot Spring.

A steel-frame cross stands in the middle of the broad concrete plaza at the summit, with a railing running around the edge. With Coron Island and Uson Island to the southwest and Coron town and its port below, this is the defining scene of the hill.

Big white letters spelling CORON stand on the slope just below the summit, to the right. The most popular shots are taken from behind the letters with the sea as a backdrop, or from the steps in front, fitting the letters and the bay into one frame.
The sun goes down over the sea between Coron Island and Uson Island, and the sky keeps changing color from about
30 minutes
before sunset until after the sun has gone. The western edge of the deck is the best spot, so claim a place early at sunset time.

After sunset the cross and the CORON letters light up, and the lights of town below and the boats in the port sparkle along with them. Looking up at the illuminated cross in the blue hour, while some blue still lingers in the sky, is a favorite scene for photographers.

blocks.title: Views of Coron Island's limestone cliffs

children.text: Across the bay, the jagged limestone peaks of Coron Island line up like a folding screen. Looking down from above and realizing that Kayangan Lake and Twin Lagoon, which you visited by boat during the day, are hidden inside them lets you picture the whole island-hopping route at a glance.

Follow the side steps a little beyond the summit and a gentle grass-covered ridge continues, open to the west, where you can watch the sunset more quietly than on the crowded deck. Another path leads down the far side to the road, but it is unlit, so walk it only in daylight.

blocks.title: Rest stops and vendors on the stairs

children.text: Rest stops with benches are spaced along the stairway, and on many days vendors sell bottled water, soft drinks, ice cream and coconuts along the way and near the summit. Some days there are no vendors, though, so it is safer to bring your own water.

items.title: Sunset route
items.subtitle: An evening climb after island hopping

children.text: Back from your island tour, freshen up at your hotel and pack 1 liter of water, a flashlight and a light layer.
Walk from town or take a tricycle (about
) to the foot of the stairs beside the basketball court.
Climb the roughly 720 steps in
20–40 minutes
, pausing at the rest stops. About three-quarters of the way up, the bay and the CORON letters come into view for the first time.
Take photos at the CORON letters first while there is still daylight, then claim a spot at the western railing of the summit cross viewing deck.
Watch the sun set toward Coron Island and Uson Island, and stay about
20 minutes
after it goes down to see the cross light up.
Switch on your flashlight, walk down slowly and have dinner at a restaurant in town.

Sunset in Coron shifts with the seasons, from around 5:30 PM (November–December) to around 6:20 PM (June–July). Check the day's sunset time and start climbing 1 to 1.5 hours before it to have plenty of time.
Arrive at the foot of the stairs before sunrise with a flashlight. Early in the morning there are few people and the air is cool.
Watch the eastern sky brighten from the summit, and after sunrise look down over Coron Island and the town in the soft light.
Walk for a while along the grassy ridge behind the summit and photograph the scenery without the crowds.
Head down, have breakfast near the market, and go to the meeting point for island tours that leave around 08:00.
Board the town tour vehicle at your hotel and visit Lualhati Park (a reclaimed seaside park) and St. Augustine Church.
Stop at a souvenir shop and a cashew shop to pick out Coron's specialty cashews.
Climb the Mount Tapyas stairs to see the viewing deck and the sunset.
Move on to Maquinit Hot Spring and end the day soaking in the warm seawater hot spring by the sea.
The order of a town tour varies by operator, and some visit the hot spring first and climb the hill later. If you really want to see the sunset from the hill, ask about the order when you book.
Since
March 29, 2026
, propeller-plane flights at Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport have moved to Clark, so there are no longer direct flights between Manila and Busuanga.
From Manila, take a P2P bus to Clark airport, about
3–3.5 hours
(about
, depending on the pickup stop and seat class), and fly from there to Busuanga Airport (USU), or connect via Cebu.
Cebgo, PAL Express and Sunlight Air fly daily to Busuanga Airport from Clark and Cebu. Routes and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
Airport routes have changed significantly recently, so be sure to check airline announcements before you go.

items.title: From the airport to Coron town

children.text: Shared vans in front of the airport take you to your hotel in Coron town for about
per person. The ride takes about
30–40 minutes
, longer if the van stops at several hotels.
There are no motorbike rentals at the airport, so rent one after you reach town.
Coron’s standard environmental tourism development fee (ETDF) is
. Register and pay for each traveler through
Coron iPASS
before arrival, then show each QR code at the verification counter. Site admission and tour charges are separate.
Large passenger ships (2GO and Atienza) sail from the port of Manila to Coron once or twice a week per operator (sailing days differ between sources, so confirm locally), taking about
11–18 hours
overnight.
Sailing days and fares change often, so check the shipping line's latest schedule, and allow for possible cancellations when seas are rough in
November–February
The foot of the stairs is about a
10–15-minute
walk from the center of Coron town. Search for "K-Heights Inn" or "Mt. Tapyas" in a map app; the starting point is in front of the basketball court right next to it.
Tricycles in town start from about
per person, about
from hotels on the edge of town, and about
or so to hire a whole tricycle.
Motorbikes rent for about
a day (based on 2023–2025 blogs; prices vary by shop, so confirm locally), and there is room to park them around the foot of the stairs. Parking for cars runs short at sunset, so arrive early.
Travel agencies' Coron town tours bundle Mount Tapyas, Lualhati Park, Maquinit Hot Spring and more for about
per person, with joiner tours commonly around
Hotel pickup is often included, which makes planning your first day easy.
The best time is the
November–May
dry season, when clear skies let you see all the way to Coron Island and the sunsets are vivid.
December–March
is peak season, so the deck gets quite crowded at sunset, and toward the end of the dry season, in
March–May
, the grass on the slopes dries out and turns the hill brown, and the stairs are very hot at midday.
In the
June–October

rainy season the hill turns green and afternoon showers are frequent, so you may miss the sunset, but clear skies right after the rain can be all the more dramatic. During the day, early morning and late afternoon are cooler, and it is best to avoid the hours around noon, when there is almost no shade.

Because the foot of the stairs is close to the middle of town, you can walk there from any hotel in Poblacion, Coron town. Small hotels and guesthouses, including K-Heights Inn right next to the stairs, cluster around this area, which suits travelers hoping to catch both the sunrise and the sunset. The port and the island-tour pier are close by too, so early tour meeting times are no trouble.

There are no restaurants on the hill, so eat after you come down. The main streets of town are lined with Filipino home-style eateries, grilled seafood spots, pizza places and Western-style cafés, and around the public market you can buy fresh fish and local specialties such as mangoes and cashews. After the sunset, have dinner in town and, if you still have energy, take a tricycle to Maquinit Hot Spring to round off the day.
To see the sunset, start climbing 1 to 1.5 hours before sundown. The prettiest colors begin about
30 minutes
before sunset and last until after the sun has gone.
Bring about 1 liter of water per person. Vendors are there on many days, but on some days there is no one at the summit.
The way down is only intermittently lit and gets dark. A headlamp is more convenient than a phone flashlight.
Sneakers or strapped sandals are enough. Some steps are uneven, so avoid flip-flops.
Rather than the crowded summit deck, the grassy ridge behind the summit opens to the west and is a good place to watch the sunset in peace.
Photograph the CORON letters while it is still light before sunset, and the cross in the blue hour after sunset when it is lit, and you will get both shots.
Climbing on your first afternoon to get a feel for the layout of Coron Island and the bay helps you understand where you are during the next day's island tour.
A sunrise walk in the morning is nearly empty and cool, great for photos and for a stair workout.
The stairs have almost no shade at midday, making heat exhaustion easy. Climb in the early morning or late afternoon, and always bring a light for the way down after dark.
The summit cross is a religious symbol. Do not climb on or lean against it for photos, and behave quietly during religious observances such as Holy Week.
After rain, the concrete steps and mossy sections are slippery. Hold the handrail and come down slowly.
The other path from behind the summit down to the road is unlit and easy to lose, so after dark go down the way you came up, by the stairs.
At sunset the summit gets crowded and spots at the railing fill up fast. Set up tripods where they do not block other people.
There are not enough trash bins, and litter sometimes piles up along the stairs. Carry your water bottles and snack wrappers back down with you.
The hill is said to have no set opening hours, but it may be closed for construction or typhoon damage, so check locally.
Coron
town, a
10–15-minute
walk from the foot of the stairs, is the hub of your trip, with island tours, wreck diving, restaurants and hotels all in one place.
A seaside saltwater hot spring about
30 minutes
from town by tricycle. The water is warm, around
, perfect for soothing your legs in the evening after the climb.
Kayangan Lake
, reached in a little over
10 minutes
by bangka boat from the town pier, is a clear lake tucked inside Coron Island, which you can see across the water from the viewing deck, and a highlight of the island tours.
At
Twin Lagoon
, you pass through a narrow gap between limestone cliffs into a second lagoon; it is often part of the same Coron Island tour.
Barracuda Lake
is an unusual lake layered with fresh water and seawater, visited by divers and snorkelers alike, and it is also a stop on Coron Island tours.
